title: LISRec: Modeling User Preferences with Learned Item Shortcuts for Sequential Recommendation

problem.claim: Sequential recommendation histories can contain noisy interactions that do not reflect genuine user preferences.

gap.claim: The approach addresses the need to distinguish stable preferences from noisy historical interactions.

contributions.claim: LISRec extracts personalized semantic shortcuts from historical interactions to model stable user preferences.
The framework learns task-agnostic semantic representations, builds a personalized semantic graph, and selects a maximal semantic connectivity subset as representative shortcuts.
The shortcut-based representation filters irrelevant actions while preserving the diversity of genuine interests.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe LISRec as a novel framework that explicitly captures stable preferences through personalized semantic shortcuts.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On the Yelp and Amazon Product datasets, LISRec reportedly improves over baseline recommendation models by 13%.
Further analysis reportedly finds that shortcut-based histories better capture user preferences and produce more accurate and relevant recommendations.
The authors report that all codes and datasets are available in a GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: Interaction histories may contain noisy actions that do not represent genuine preferences.
LISRec introduces personalized semantic shortcuts to capture stable preferences.
The method constructs a semantic graph and selects its maximal semantic connectivity subset as representative shortcuts.
The focused representation is intended to remove irrelevant actions while preserving diverse interests.
Experiments and further analysis report improved recommendation performance and preference capture.
